prompt: Explain the greenhouse effect and why adding greenhouse gases warms the planet.
hook: The greenhouse effect is natural; the problem is turning it up.

card.oneLiner: Greenhouse gases trap some of the heat Earth would otherwise radiate to space, and adding more of them warms the planet and shifts the climate.
keyPoints: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life.
Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests add carbon dioxide and methane.
More trapped heat raises the global average temperature.
Warming drives heatwaves, heavier rainfall and sea-level rise.

framework.name: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6)
framework.gloss: Human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land at a rate unprecedented in millennia.

framework.name: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
framework.gloss: The objective is to stabilise greenhouse-gas concentrations in the atmosphere.

whatYouCanDo: Learn the main gases: carbon dioxide from fuels, methane from waste and livestock.
Follow India's official greenhouse-gas inventory for the national picture.
Explain the effect in plain language to someone who is unsure.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Key numbers update with each assessment cycle.

sources.title: IPCC — Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

prompt: Explain what 1.5°C of warming means and why the target matters.
hook: Half a degree is not a rounding error.

card.oneLiner: The Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to pursue 1.5°C, because every fraction of a degree raises the risk of extreme impacts.
keyPoints: The world has already warmed by more than 1°C above pre-industrial levels.
The difference between 1.5°C and 2°C is large for heatwaves, reefs and sea level.
Staying at 1.5°C needs rapid, deep cuts in emissions.
Even with overshoot, the peak temperature and duration matter.

framework.name: IPCC Special Report on 1.5°C
framework.gloss: Impacts are greater at 2°C than at 1.5°C across most systems.

framework.name: Paris Agreement
framework.gloss: Hold the global temperature rise well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C.

whatYouCanDo: Track the current warming level from an official monitoring source.
Compare India's pledged targets with the 1.5°C pathway.
Discuss adaptation and mitigation together, not as alternatives.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Reported warming figures are updated as records are revised.

prompt: Explain the carbon budget and what net zero means.
hook: Net zero means the taps balance the drains.

card.oneLiner: The carbon budget is the total carbon dioxide we can still emit to stay under a temperature limit, and net zero means not adding to the total.
keyPoints: Warming depends on cumulative emissions, not the rate in a single year.
The remaining budget for 1.5°C is small and shrinking.
Net zero means emissions released equal emissions removed.
India has pledged net zero by 2070.

framework.name: IPCC AR6
framework.gloss: Every tonne of carbon dioxide adds to warming.

framework.name: India's net zero pledge
framework.gloss: India committed to reach net zero emissions by 2070.

whatYouCanDo: Distinguish gross emissions from net emissions when you read targets.
Ask how removals such as forests are counted versus real cuts.
Follow India's Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Budget estimates are uncertain and revised by researchers.

sources.title: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

prompt: Explain the difference between weather and climate, and how scientists detect a climate trend.
hook: Weather is your mood; climate is your personality.

card.oneLiner: Weather is the short-term condition of the atmosphere, while climate is the long-term pattern, and long records reveal the slow trend beneath the noise.
keyPoints: Weather changes hour to hour; climate is measured over decades.
A cold day does not disprove a warming climate.
Scientists separate natural variability from a forced trend.
Attribution studies link individual events to warming.
whatYouCanDo: Look at decadal averages rather than a single season.
Use official data when arguing about trends.
Be careful not to confuse a single weather event with the overall trend.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Local trends can differ from the global average.

prompt: Explain how climate change is affecting the Indian monsoon.
hook: The monsoon is changing, not disappearing.

card.oneLiner: Warming is making the monsoon more erratic, with longer dry spells and heavier bursts, even as the total seasonal rainfall varies from year to year.
keyPoints: Rainfall is arriving in fewer, more intense spells.
Dry spells within the season are lengthening.
Changes differ across regions and can be masked by year-to-year swings.
Shifts matter for farming, reservoirs and flood risk.

framework.name: IPCC AR6
framework.gloss: Projected increases in heavy precipitation for South Asia.

whatYouCanDo: Follow official seasonal forecasts before planning crops or water use.
Plan for both dry spells and intense downpours in the same season.
Support rainwater storage and drainage that tolerate extremes.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Monsoon projections carry high uncertainty.
